hints: Notice the two big clues together, steamy fumes means acidic $HCl$ gas is released by hydrolysis, and the white solid must be a hydroxide or oxide.
A white precipitate that dissolves in both $NaOH(aq)$ and $HCl(aq)$ is a classic sign of an amphoteric hydroxide, so think which Period 3 metal forms one.
Check which chloride hydrolyses with a little water to give that amphoteric hydroxide plus $HCl$ fumes, and rule out the chlorides that give only a solution or an acidic oxide.
walkthrough:
**Decode what steamy fumes tells us**

Think hydrolysis, not just dissolving. When a covalent Period 3 chloride meets a small amount of water, it reacts vigorously to release $HCl(g)$, seen as white steamy fumes.

General idea:
$$\text{chloride} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{hydroxide or oxide (white solid)} + HCl$$

**Decode what the white precipitate tells us**

The solid dissolves in both $NaOH(aq)$ and $HCl(aq)$. That is the textbook test for amphoteric.

That points straight to aluminium hydroxide:
$$\text{Al(OH)}_3(s) + OH^- \rightarrow [\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$$
$$\text{Al(OH)}_3(s) + 3H^+ \rightarrow \text{Al}^{3+} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Put it together for element E**

Aluminium chloride hydrolyses exactly in this way with a little water to give a white precipitate and fumes:
$$\text{AlCl}_3(s) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3(s) + 3HCl(g)$$
That matches all three observations, so E is aluminium.

options.A: Magnesium chloride, $MgCl_2$, simply dissolves in water to give a colourless solution of $Mg^{2+}$ and $Cl^-$. It does not hydrolyse to give steamy $HCl$ fumes and a white precipitate, and $Mg(OH)_2$ is basic only, soluble in acid but not in $NaOH(aq)$.
options.B: Aluminium chloride hydrolyses with a small amount of water: $AlCl_3 + 3H_2O \rightarrow Al(OH)_3(s) + 3HCl(g)$. The $Al(OH)_3$ is a white precipitate and the $HCl$ is the steamy fumes. $Al(OH)_3$ is amphoteric so it dissolves in both $NaOH(aq)$ and $HCl(aq)$.
options.C: Silicon tetrachloride, $SiCl_4$, does hydrolyse with steamy fumes: $SiCl_4 + 2H_2O \rightarrow SiO_2 + 4HCl$. However the white solid is silicon dioxide, $SiO_2$, which is acidic, not amphoteric. It will dissolve in hot concentrated $NaOH$ but will not dissolve in $HCl(aq)$.
options.D: Phosphorus chlorides such as $PCl_3$ and $PCl_5$ hydrolyse to give steamy fumes of $HCl$, but the phosphorus product is an acid like $H_3PO_3$ or $H_3PO_4$, which stays in solution. No white amphoteric precipitate is formed.
